programs.title: VOA's 60th Anniversary
programs.credit: Voice of America — THIS IS AMERICA (Special English), Feb. 11, 2002 · Public Domain
paragraphs: February Twenty-Fourth marks the sixtieth {anniversary} of the first {broadcast} on the Voice of America. This year, VOA will be honoring its past and looking forward to its future.

The world has changed much since the first VOA broadcast sixty years ago. When listeners first heard VOA on that February day in Nineteen-Forty-Two, the United States had recently entered World War Two. The country was fighting against Germany and Japan.

American officials believed they should answer the German broadcasts with the {truthful} account of world events. The first VOA broadcast was a short report in the German language. It began with these words: "Here speak voices from America. Everyday at this time we will bring you the news of the war. The news may be good. The news may be bad. We shall tell you the truth."
Since then, the Voice of America has {expanded} to include more than one-thousand employees. They produce more than one-thousand hours of programs every week. VOA broadcasts in fifty-three languages.

In Nineteen-Fifty-Nine, VOA added another new kind of program to its broadcasts. VOA officials invented a simpler kind of English. It uses about one-thousand-five-hundred words, spoken slowly. Of course, you are listening to it now: Special English.

The law contains a statement of what the Voice of America must do. First, VOA will present news that is truthful, fair and complete. Second, VOA will present a {balanced} picture of all sides of American life. And third, VOA will present the policies of the United States government, as well as opinions supporting and opposing those policies.

gloss.anniversary: the date on which an event happened in a previous year
gloss.broadcast: to send out a program on radio or television
gloss.expanded: became larger in size, number, or scope
gloss.balanced: giving fair and equal treatment to all sides

programs.title: A Vaccine Campaign Against Meningitis
programs.credit: Voice of America — SCIENCE IN THE NEWS #2131 (Special English), July 3, 2001 · Public Domain (excerpt)
paragraphs: This is Bob Doughty. And this is Sarah Long with SCIENCE IN THE NEWS, a VOA Special English program about recent developments in science. Today, we tell about a campaign to develop a {vaccine} to prevent the disease meningitis in Africa.

For years, scientists believed it was possible to develop a vaccine to prevent the deadly disease meningitis in Africa. However, it costs a great deal of money for drug companies to research and test such a vaccine. Recently the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation gave seventy-million dollars for a project to develop a vaccine to end meningitis in southern Africa.

The World Health Organization and a health technology company in Seattle, Washington, will work with drug companies on the ten-year project. Such research is {profitable} when demand for the vaccines is great and rich countries are willing to pay for the drugs. In very poor countries, however, the market for medicines is very small.

Meningitis is an infection of the brain caused by a {bacterium}. The disease is most common among young people. Babies are most at risk. The disease can be treated with {antibiotic} drugs. But even when treated, at least ten percent of the victims die.

More than seven-hundred-thousand cases of meningitis were reported in Africa between Nineteen-Eighty-Eight and Nineteen-Ninety-Seven. The largest recorded {epidemic} was in Nineteen-Ninety-Six, with more than two-hundred-thousand cases and twenty-thousand deaths.

gloss.vaccine: a substance given to the body to protect it from a disease
gloss.bacterium: a very small living thing (singular of 'bacteria') that can cause disease
gloss.antibiotic: a medicine that fights infections caused by bacteria
gloss.epidemic: an outbreak of a disease that spreads quickly to many people

programs.title: Learning English Expressions or Idioms
programs.credit: Voice of America — Ask a Teacher, VOA Learning English (by Andrew Smith) · Public Domain
paragraphs: This week on Ask a Teacher, we consider expressions, or {idioms}, and offer some advice for learning them.

An idiom is an expression formed from two or more words. But an idiom's meaning often cannot be understood just by knowing each of the words in it. Let's look at an example: We want our students to think outside the box.

Here, the words outside the box form an idiom. People use idioms in connection to situations, so they usually say more than one sentence to help you understand: We want our students to think outside the box. That's why we push them to find {creative} ways to solve problems.

Here is some advice: avoid {translating} idioms word-for-word into your native language. When you hear a short group of words that seem unrelated to the subject, those words will often be an idiom. And be sure to learn the {tone} an idiom carries — the best way is to ask native speakers.

With thousands of idioms in English, there is a lot to learn. But do not throw in the towel, in other words, do not give up. Instead, knock yourself out, or try hard, and do your best to learn them. And you will feel proud as a {peacock}!

gloss.idioms: expressions whose meaning is different from the meanings of the individual words
gloss.translating: changing words from one language into another
gloss.tone: the feeling or attitude that a word or expression carries
gloss.peacock: a large, brightly colored bird — 'proud as a peacock' means very proud

programs.title: Crocuses Are Blooming Early — What This Means for Nature
programs.credit: Lionel Smith, Anglia Ruskin University — republished from The Conversation under CC BY-ND
paragraphs: Amid the wet and grey gloom of February, gardeners across the UK are reporting that crocuses are pushing through their lawns and borders weeks ahead of schedule. This phenomenon is no quirk of nature. Crocuses flowering early in 2026 is a sign of shifting seasons, driven by a unique combination of biological triggers and record-breaking UK weather patterns.

Crocuses are {thermoperiodic} plants, which means they rely on temperature cues rather than day length to dictate their lifecycle. Their {corms} also usually need a cold spell in autumn to prompt an annual reset before they will start to grow toward flowering around March.

In a typical year, this process unfolds gradually. But if soil temperatures stay mild in autumn and through December and January, as they have this winter, the reset button is not hit and crocuses can reach their flowering threshold far sooner, emerging in late January and early February rather than March.

No cold reset usually means a "blind" corm — one that produces leaves but no flowers. Met Office data shows the UK has three weeks fewer ground frosts annually compared to 50 years ago, preventing some plants from entering their normal state of {dormancy} over winter.

There are other influences beyond climate change that may {amplify} this early flowering. City plants can bloom days earlier than rural ones, as concrete and asphalt trap daytime heat. Light pollution in cities may mimic longer days, disrupting plant circadian rhythms. And soil microbiome communities that thrive in warmer weather may boost flowering too.

This early crocus bloom may seem delightful after months of drab grey winter, but gardeners should be wary of weather reversals. Buds and flowers are more exposed if colder conditions return, meaning they may wither. Their purple and yellow petals, pushing through in January and February rather than March, are as clear a signal as any thermometer.

gloss.thermoperiodic: responding to changes in temperature rather than day length
gloss.corms: underground plant stems that store food, similar to bulbs
gloss.dormancy: a resting state in which growth and activity slow down or stop
gloss.amplify: to increase the size, strength, or effect of something
